title: 7 Best Deck Stains in 2026: Penetrating Oil vs Solid Color
metaDescription: Armstrong Clark semi-transparent is the best deck stain for most decks: it soaks in, fades instead of peeling and recoats without stripping. 6 more picks.
keywords: what is the best deck stain
intro:
The best deck stain for most pressure-treated pine, cedar and redwood decks is Armstrong Clark semi-transparent, a penetrating oil that soaks into the wood, wears by fading rather than peeling, and recoats without stripping. For a tired, gray, patched deck, a solid stain such as Olympic Maximum hides the damage, but it trades away that easy maintenance.

When a deck finish fails, the product is rarely the real culprit. They come from putting a film-forming stain where a penetrating oil belonged, staining boards that were still wet, or choosing a clear finish for a deck in full sun. Settle the opacity and the oil-or-water question for your particular boards, and picking a brand becomes simple. This guide ranks seven stains, then covers prep, application, coverage, climate and how often to recoat.
quickAnswer: Buy Armstrong Clark for the best all-round deck stain and sealer on softwood, Ready Seal if you are nervous about lap marks, TWP 100 Series for damp and shaded decks, and DEFY Extreme if you want water-based. Use Cabot Australian Timber Oil on hardwoods, Olympic Maximum Solid on weathered boards, and Behr Premium Transparent only for shaded decks on a budget.

sections.heading: Best Deck Stain: The Short Answer
sections.body:
**Armstrong Clark semi-transparent** is the best deck stain for most softwood decks, because a penetrating oil protects against sun and water and recoats with a wash and one thin coat. **Ready Seal** is the most forgiving to apply, and **DEFY Extreme** is the best water-based option.

| Stain | Best for | Key spec |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Armstrong Clark | Most softwood decks | Oil-based penetrating, semi-transparent or semi-solid |
| Ready Seal | First-time stainers, spraying | Oil-based, no back-brushing per label |
| TWP 100 Series | Damp, shaded, mildew-prone decks | Registered wood preservative with mildewcide |
| DEFY Extreme | Low odor, strict VOC states | Water-based, zinc oxide UV blockers |
| Cabot Australian Timber Oil | Ipe, mahogany and other hardwoods | Translucent linseed and tung oil blend |
| Olympic Maximum Solid | Weathered, patched decks | Water-based solid color, hides grain |
| Behr Premium Transparent | Budget, shaded decks | Water-based clear water repellent |

If you are unsure, choose a semi-transparent penetrating stain in a mid-tone color. It is the most forgiving choice on pressure-treated pine and cedar, and you can always move to a heavier pigment later, while going from solid back to semi-transparent means stripping to bare wood.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Deck Stains in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
These picks are ranked on published manufacturer data (opacity, resin type, coverage, VOC compliance and recoat guidance), on what each product is designed to do, and on recurring patterns in owner reports about peeling, fading and maintenance. No lab trials were run for this guide, and no product paid for placement.

### Best Overall: Armstrong Clark Wood Stain (Semi-Transparent)
Armstrong Clark blends drying oils, which harden in the wood, with non-drying oils that stay flexible and keep feeding the fibers. The result sinks into the surface instead of forming a film on top, which is exactly what a horizontal deck floor needs. When it wears, it thins and lightens rather than flaking, so the next maintenance coat is a cleaning, a light brightening and another thin application, with no stripping. The semi-transparent version leaves the grain visible with enough color to hold off graying; the semi-solid version evens out older, patchy boards while still soaking in, so it avoids the flaking that solid stains are known for. Owners commonly report two to three seasons on deck floors before a refresh, with railings lasting longer. It suits pressure-treated pine, cedar and redwood. The downsides are availability, since you may need to order online, a price above store brands and mineral-spirits cleanup.

**Pros:** Penetrates instead of filming; fades evenly; recoats without stripping; semi-solid option.
**Cons:** Harder to find in big-box stores; costs more per gallon; oil cleanup.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Armstrong+Clark+deck+stain+semi-transparent&tag=sktiger-20)

### Easiest to Apply: Ready Seal Exterior Stain and Sealer
Ready Seal's reputation rests on forgiveness. The label says it needs no back-brushing or primer and is formulated to avoid lap marks, so you can spray or roll a section, stop for lunch and pick up again without a visible line. That makes it a natural choice for a first deck project or a large area you plan to spray with a pump or airless sprayer. Natural Cedar is the best-selling color, a warm mid-tone on pine and pressure-treated lumber that looks orange for the first few days and settles into its final shade over about two weeks as the solvent leaves the wood. The trade-off is durability on high-exposure surfaces: owners in hot, sunny climates often report needing a refresh after one to two years, especially on south-facing floors. The upside is that a refresh is only a cleaning and another coat.

**Pros:** No back-brushing per label; resists lap marks; sprays easily; recoats without stripping.
**Cons:** Looks orange at first; lighter pigment wears faster in sun; solvent smell.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ready+Seal+Natural+Cedar&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Damp, Shaded Decks: TWP 100 Series
TWP stands for Total Wood Preservative, and the 100 Series is registered as a wood preservative, carrying mildewcides and fungicides rather than serving only as a cosmetic coating. If your deck sits under trees, faces north or stays damp into the afternoon, the green and black growth that returns every spring is the real problem, and this product is built for it. It is a penetrating oil that soaks into rough-sawn and smooth boards alike, with classic colors such as Cedartone and Redwood, and deck restoration contractors have used it for decades. The catch is regulatory: the 100 Series exceeds VOC limits in some states, where buyers get the compliant 1500 Series instead. Apply it thin, with two wet-on-wet coats on very thirsty wood, and plan on a light maintenance coat every couple of years.

**Pros:** Mildew and fungal protection; penetrates rough and smooth lumber; long contractor track record.
**Cons:** Not sold in every state; strong odor; two coats on dry wood.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=TWP+100+Series+deck+stain&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Water-Based: DEFY Extreme Semi-Transparent
DEFY Extreme from Saver Systems is the water-based stain that oil loyalists tend to respect. It relies on nano-sized zinc oxide, the sunscreen ingredient, to block UV, which helps its color last longer than typical latex deck stains. It dries quickly, cleans up with water and carries a low-VOC formula that is legal in every state, so it suits strict air-quality areas and anyone staining next to an occupied house with windows open. It behaves more like a penetrating finish than a paint and is designed to be recoated without stripping. Two cautions apply. Because it sets up quickly, stain in the shade and keep each pass blending into wet stain, or overlaps will show. And water-based finishes forgive dirty or mill-glazed wood less, so cleaning and brightening are not optional. Done right, owners commonly report two years or more on a deck floor.

**Pros:** Zinc oxide UV protection; low odor, water cleanup; legal in every state; one-day job.
**Cons:** Lap marks in hot weather; demands careful prep; wears faster on busy walkways.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DEFY+Extreme+semi-transparent+wood+stain&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Hardwoods: Cabot Australian Timber Oil
Cabot Australian Timber Oil is made for dense tropical hardwoods that shrug off most stains. Its oil blend, which includes linseed and tung oils, penetrates tight-grained species such as ipe, cumaru and mahogany better than heavy-bodied stains that sit on top and turn tacky. The translucent finish adds warmth while letting the grain dominate, and colors such as Honey Teak, Natural and Mahogany Flame enrich rather than mask the wood. It also works on cedar and redwood when you want a richer look than a clear sealer gives, and it is easy to find at paint and home stores. Light pigment means less UV shielding, so a sun-baked deck will want a fresh coat every year or two. Apply one thin coat, wipe puddles within the label's window and skip a heavy second coat on dense wood, the most common cause of a sticky finish.

**Pros:** Penetrates dense hardwoods; translucent grain-forward look; widely available.
**Cons:** Frequent recoats in full sun; slow drying in cool, humid weather; tacky if overapplied.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Cabot+Australian+Timber+Oil&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Solid Deck Stain: Olympic Maximum Stain + Sealant in One (Solid)
A solid stain is the honest fix for a tired deck. If your boards are patched, mismatched or carry a gray cast that cleaning will not lift, Olympic Maximum Solid covers it all in a uniform color while leaving some wood texture. It is tinted in store in a broad range of shades, and its heavy pigment load gives the strongest UV blocking on this list. Like any solid color, it builds a skin on the wood, and on a walking surface that skin eventually cracks and lifts where water sits and shoes scuff. That peeling risk is what keeps it out of the top spots. Use it where it shines, on rails, fascia and other vertical parts, and put it on floors only when the boards are clean and bone dry. Commit knowing you will stay with solid colors, because stripping it back to bare wood is a weekend of hard labor.

**Pros:** Hides gray and patched boards; wide color range; strongest UV blocking; easy touch-ups.
**Cons:** Film can peel on floors; hides grain; very hard to go back to transparent.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Olympic+Maximum+solid+deck+stain&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: Behr Premium Transparent Waterproofing Wood Finish
Behr Premium Transparent is the budget pick, and it does one job well: it makes water bead and keeps moisture out of the boards, which limits cracking and checking. Because it is clear, brand-new cedar or redwood keeps its natural color, and the water-based formula means low odor and easy cleanup. Sunlight is another matter. UV attacks the lignin at the surface of the wood regardless of how well water beads, so an untinted coat on a sunny deck still fades to silver within a season or two. That makes it a fit for covered porches, shaded decks and owners happy to recoat every year, which is quick and cheap with this product. For color retention on a sunny deck, step up to a semi-transparent with real pigment, including Behr's own tinted versions.

**Pros:** Low cost per gallon; water-based and low odor; keeps new wood's natural color.
**Cons:** Little UV protection; wood still grays in sun; needs yearly recoats.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Behr+Premium+Transparent+Waterproofing+Wood+Finish&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Which Deck Stain Opacity Should You Choose?
sections.body:
Choose semi-transparent for most softwood decks, semi-solid for older or blotchy boards, and solid only for weathered decks you no longer want to show off. Pigment sets the trade: more pigment blocks more UV, the main force that grays and breaks down the wood surface, while less pigment shows more grain.

| Opacity | Grain visible | Typical floor life | Best use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Clear or toner | All | About 1 year | Shaded decks, new cedar |
| Semi-transparent | Most | 2 to 3 years | Most softwood decks |
| Semi-solid | Some texture | 2 to 4 years | Older or uneven boards |
| Solid | Texture only | 3 to 5 years, may peel | Weathered decks, railings |

These ranges come from manufacturer guidance and contractor experience; sun and foot traffic move your deck up or down.

### What is the best solid deck stain?
Olympic Maximum Solid is the strongest pick for covering a worn deck, with heavy pigment and broad color choice. Keep in mind that solid stains do not fail gracefully: when the film lets go on a floor it peels in patches, which means scraping and sanding before you can recoat.

### What deck stain color lasts the longest?
Medium shades like cedar, redwood and light brown in semi-transparent or semi-solid opacity last longest. They carry enough pigment to block UV and hide dirt and wear. Clear and very light finishes fade fastest, and very dark solids show scuffs and get hot underfoot.

sections.heading: Oil-Based vs Water-Based Deck Stain: Which Is Better?
sections.body:
Oil-based penetrating stain is the safer default for a first-time softwood deck project; water-based is better for strict VOC states, one-day jobs and staining next to an occupied house.

### What is the best oil based deck stain?
Armstrong Clark is the best oil-based deck stain for most decks, with Ready Seal close behind for ease of application and TWP 100 Series for mildew-prone sites. Oil stains carry pigment deep into the wood, rarely show lap marks and wear by fading rather than peeling. The costs are odor, mineral-spirits cleanup, slow drying in cool weather and VOC limits on some formulas.

### What is the best water based deck stain?
DEFY Extreme leads the water-based field thanks to its zinc oxide UV blockers and low-VOC formula. Modern water-based stains dry fast, smell mild, clean up with soap and water and hold color well. Many sit closer to the surface, though, so on a horizontal floor they are more likely to wear unevenly or flake if the wood was dirty or not fully dry.

### Can you switch from oil to water-based?
Not directly. Do not put oil over a film-forming water-based stain, and do not put a water-based penetrating stain over a fresh oil coat; either can fail to bond. When you switch chemistry, strip the deck or let the old finish weather off almost completely.

### What about Sherwin-Williams deck stain?
Sherwin-Williams sells its own deck stain lines through its stores. Judge any store brand on the same points used here: opacity, oil or water base, recoat guidance on the label and whether it fades or peels as it wears.

sections.heading: How Do You Match a Stain to Your Deck Wood?
sections.body:
Species, age and existing finish narrow the choice fast.

### Pressure-treated pine
The most common US deck lumber arrives wet from treatment and must dry before it accepts stain, often several weeks to a few months. It takes semi-transparent oils well, which is why so many top stains come in cedar and redwood tones. Drip a little water on it; when the drops disappear into the wood within minutes, you can stain.

### Cedar and redwood
These softer, porous woods are full of natural extractives. They absorb unevenly if overloaded and can bleed tannins through water-based finishes. A light penetrating oil in a toned color that echoes the wood looks best, and a clear water repellent from our [exterior wood sealer picks](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/) suits new boards you want to keep natural for a season.

### Tropical hardwoods
Ipe, cumaru and garapa are too dense for ordinary stains. Use a hardwood oil such as Cabot Australian Timber Oil, apply it very thin and expect yearly recoats. Many owners simply let hardwood weather to silver and clean it once a year.

### Old decks with an existing finish
An evenly worn semi-transparent oil normally accepts a fresh coat of the same product once the deck is cleaned. A peeling solid stain must be stripped or sanded first. If boards are cupped, split or soft, replace them before spending on any coating, or consider a heavier resurfacer from our [deck paint rankings](/best-deck-paint/).

sections.heading: How Do You Prep and Apply Deck Stain Without Streaks?
sections.body:
Clean, brighten, dry and sand lightly, then stain in shade in thin coats, a few boards at a time. Manufacturers say plainly in their data sheets that a stain is only as good as the surface under it.

### How do you clean the deck?
Use an oxygen-bleach (sodium percarbonate) deck cleaner for dirt, mildew and gray fibers, or a stripper made for your old coating. Rinse with a garden hose or a pressure washer on low with a wide fan tip held at least 12 inches away; high pressure furs the grain. A [pressure washer surface cleaner](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) speeds up large floors.

### Why use a brightener?
An oxalic or citric acid brightener neutralizes cleaner residue, removes tannin and rust marks and opens the grain so stain absorbs evenly. Skipping it is the top cause of a blotchy result.

### How dry should the wood be?
Give the boards two full days to dry after washing, and more if it rains. Water drops should soak in within minutes, and many labels target a pin-meter reading under about 15 percent. Knock down raised fibers with 60 to 80 grit on a pole sander, no finer.

### How do you apply it?
Most labels want 50 to 90 degrees Fahrenheit, no rain for 24 hours and no direct midday sun. Do railings first, then the floor two or three boards at a time along their full length, stopping only at board ends. Spray or roll, then back-brush immediately, and wipe off anything that has not soaked in after the time on the can, usually 15 to 30 minutes. A heavy second coat on saturated wood stays tacky and peels.

sections.heading: How Much Deck Stain Do You Need, and What Does It Cost?
sections.body:
Plan around the low end of the label's coverage range. Typical labels list roughly 100 to 250 square feet per gallon on weathered wood and 150 to 300 on smooth new boards, and railings, balusters and stairs use about half again as much per square foot as the floor.

### How do you estimate gallons?
Measure the floor, add stair faces and an estimate of railing surface, then divide by the low coverage number. A common 12 by 16 foot deck with a simple rail usually takes 2 to 3 gallons of penetrating stain for one coat. A 5-gallon pail is often cheaper per gallon near that amount and keeps one color batch.

### What does staining a deck cost?
Retail gallons run from budget water-based products at the low end to premium penetrating oils at roughly twice that, and cleaner, brightener and a good brush or sprayer add to the bill. Hiring it out typically runs a few dollars per square foot in contractor quotes, plus extra for stripping or board repairs. On a 200 square foot deck, the gap between budget and premium stain is usually modest compared with how much longer the better finish lasts.

### Why test a sample first?
Color shifts dramatically with species, age and absorption. Test a quart on a prepped board in a hidden corner and let it dry fully before buying gallons.

sections.heading: How Do Climate and Exposure Change the Best Deck Stain?
sections.body:
Sun calls for pigment, shade calls for mildew resistance and freeze-thaw climates call for penetrating stains.

### Hot, sunny climates
UV is the main enemy, so a semi-transparent or semi-solid in a mid-tone protects far better than clear or very light finishes. South and west-facing floors wear fastest, so inspect them first each spring.

### Humid or shaded decks
Moisture and mildew rule. Choose a stain with mildewcide such as TWP, keep leaf litter off the boards and make sure air moves under the deck. Some water-based formulas are less prone to feeding surface mildew than natural-oil stains.

### Freeze-thaw climates
Water gets under film-forming finishes through cracks, freezes and lifts the coating. Penetrating stains have no film to lift and let wood dry between storms, which limits cracking and cupping.

### VOC rules
Several states and air districts cap VOC content, so some classic oil formulas are not sold there. Makers usually offer a compliant series, and the gap has narrowed.

sections.heading: How Often Should You Restain a Deck, and When Is Sealer or Paint Better?
sections.body:
Most deck floors need a maintenance coat every two to three years with a semi-transparent stain, every year with clear or toner, and every three to five years with solid stain. Railings and fascia last longer because they get less sun and no foot traffic.

| Task | How often | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sweep and clear gaps | Monthly in season | Prevents trapped moisture |
| Wash with deck cleaner | Every spring | Oxygen-based, low pressure |
| Recoat floor and stairs | Every 1 to 3 years | Sooner with clear or light stains |
| Recoat railings and fascia | Every 3 to 5 years | Less sun and wear |

### How do you know it is time?
Once water soaks in instead of beading and the walking paths look washed out, wash, brighten, let it dry and lay down a single thin coat of what you used before. Film-forming finishes need spot scraping and touch-ups before water gets under them. Keep a sealed quart and a note of the product and color for touch-ups.

### When is a sealer the better choice?
A clear water repellent costs less per year on a covered porch or new cedar you want to keep natural, as long as you recoat annually. Our [deck sealant guide](/best-deck-sealant/) compares the clear options.

### When is deck paint better?
Thick resurfacing coatings hide damage on old but structurally sound boards, though as film-formers they can trap moisture and peel. For fences and pergolas, which take far less abuse, see our [fence stain picks](/best-fence-stain/).

mistakes.title: Staining over a peeling finish
mistakes.body: Fresh stain has nothing solid to grip when the layer under it is coming loose. It adds weight to the failing film and peels off with it, usually within a season. Remove every loose patch down to firm wood, brighten, and wait for the boards to dry before you recoat.

mistakes.title: Working in full midday sun
mistakes.body: Hot boards flash-dry stain before it soaks in, leaving lap marks, uneven color and a thin layer that wears fast. Begin in morning shade, move with the shadows as the day goes on, and quit when the boards feel too hot to rest your hand on.

mistakes.title: Skipping the brightener
mistakes.body: Cleaners and strippers leave wood alkaline and darkened, and stain absorbs unevenly on that surface. A brightener resets the pH, lifts tannin and rust marks and opens the grain. It costs little, takes minutes and often makes the biggest visible difference.

mistakes.title: Piling on a heavy second coat
mistakes.body: Wood can only take in so much penetrating stain. Anything beyond that point stays on the surface as a sticky layer for days, then scuffs off or flakes in patches. Apply thin coats, back-brush and wipe anything still glossy after the time on the label.

mistakes.title: Choosing color from a paper chip
mistakes.body: The same stain looks completely different on new pine, weathered cedar and redwood, and chips only hint at the result. Buy a sample, test it on a prepped board in a hidden spot and let it dry fully before you buy gallons for the whole deck.

faqs.q: What is the best deck stain?
faqs.a: Armstrong Clark semi-transparent is the best deck stain for most softwood decks because it penetrates instead of forming a film, fades evenly and recoats without stripping. Ready Seal is the easiest to apply, DEFY Extreme is the best water-based option and Olympic Maximum Solid is the pick for covering a weathered deck.

faqs.q: What is the best deck stain and sealer in one?
faqs.a: Armstrong Clark and Ready Seal both work as a stain and sealer in one, combining pigment for UV protection with oils that repel water. Olympic Maximum Stain + Sealant in One does the same as a solid color. Clear products seal out water but offer little sun protection, so decks finished with them still gray.

faqs.q: What is the most durable deck stain?
faqs.a: Solid stains such as Olympic Maximum block the most UV and can last three to five years on a floor, but they peel when they fail. For durability with easy upkeep, a semi-transparent or semi-solid penetrating oil such as Armstrong Clark is the better choice, because it fades evenly and recoats without stripping.

faqs.q: Should I use an oil-based or water-based deck stain?
faqs.a: Oil penetrating stains forgive more mistakes: they absorb deeply, hide overlaps and wear away gradually instead of flaking. Water-based products dry quicker, have little odor, wash out of brushes with water and meet VOC rules nationwide. Either works on a well-prepped deck, but do not switch types without stripping.

faqs.q: How often should you stain a deck?
faqs.a: Most decks need a fresh coat on the floor every two to three years with semi-transparent stain, every year with a clear or toner finish, and every three to five years with solid stain. Sunny, south-facing decks and heavy traffic shorten that. Recoat when water stops beading and the traffic paths fade.

faqs.q: How long should you wait to stain a new deck?
faqs.a: It depends on the lumber. Kiln-dried boards can often be stained within weeks, while wet pressure-treated pine usually needs several weeks to a few months, longer in humid climates. Splash some water on a board; if it absorbs within minutes you can stain, and if it beads up, give it more time and retest.

faqs.q: Can you put new deck stain over old stain?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the existing finish is a penetrating stain that has faded evenly with no flaking. Wash and brighten, wait for the wood to dry, then apply the same product or one designed to go over it. If the old finish is a peeling solid stain or film, strip or sand the loose areas first, and strip before switching from oil to water-based.

bottomLine: For most softwood decks, the best deck stain is a semi-transparent penetrating oil such as Armstrong Clark or Ready Seal: it guards against sun and water, fades instead of peeling and recoats with a wash and one thin coat. Choose DEFY Extreme for water-based, TWP 100 Series where mildew is the enemy, Cabot Australian Timber Oil for hardwoods and Olympic Maximum Solid only for a deck that is past showing off its grain. Whatever you buy, put more effort into prep than into the brand: clean, brighten, let the wood dry, test a sample and stain in the shade in thin coats.
